 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Performance"],
 "sports":["Rugby"],
 "populations":["Healthy Athletes","Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary":"In this randomized trial with no control group, 21 premier league rugby union players completed an 8-week Nordic hamstring exercise program either at a constant workload or with progressive workload. Only the progressive group improved concentric and eccentric hamstring peak torque (7 to 8%, small effects) and the conventional and functional hamstring-to-quadriceps ratios (6 to 7%, moderate effects). Both groups increased biceps femoris long head thickness (about 7%) and fascicle length (about 7% and 10%), and no between-group difference reached statistical significance.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The trial is small (21 players from one squad), has no control group, and does not measure injury incidence, which the authors could not follow across the season. No between-group difference was statistically significant, so the advantage of progressive workload rests on magnitude-based inference and the outcomes are risk-factor measures rather than injuries.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could take the title's claim that progressive workload maximizes the program as established, when the between-group differences were not statistically significant in 21 players and the injury outcome was not measured.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2018,
   "citation":"Severo-Silveira L, Dornelles MP, Lima-e-Silva FX, Marchiori CL, Medeiros TM, Pappas E, et al. Progressive Workload Periodization Maximizes Effects of Nordic Hamstring Exercise on Muscle Injury Risk Factors. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2018.",
   "doi":"10.1519/jsc.0000000000002849",
   "abstract":"The study compared constant and progressive workload 8-week Nordic hamstring exercise programs in 21 rugby union players on hamstring strength and biceps femoris long head architecture. Only the progressive group increased hamstring strength and hamstring-to-quadriceps ratios, while both groups increased muscle thickness and fascicle length. The authors conclude that progressive workload was superior for strength and fascicle length, although the between-group differences were not statistically significant.",
   "tldr":"Nordic hamstring training improved hamstring muscle size and length in these rugby players whether the workload was constant or progressive. Only the progressive program also improved hamstring strength and hamstring-to-quadriceps ratios, but the between-group differences were not statistically significant.",
   "methods":"Twenty-one rugby union players were randomized to a constant or progressive workload 8-week Nordic hamstring exercise program, with two sessions per week and no control group. Isokinetic knee strength and biceps femoris long head thickness, pennation angle and fascicle length (ultrasound) were measured within one week before and after the program, and within-group changes were compared with magnitude-based inference.",
   "findings":"Only the progressive group increased concentric hamstring peak torque (7.7%, p = 0.004, d = 0.42) and eccentric hamstring peak torque (6.9%, p = 0.041, d = 0.39), along with conventional (7.6%, p = 0.015) and functional (6.6%, p = 0.026) hamstring-to-quadriceps ratios. Both groups increased biceps femoris long head thickness (about 7%) and fascicle length, with the constant group rising from 10.48 to 11.26 cm and the progressive group from 11.13 to 12.26 cm. No between-group difference was statistically significant.",
   "limitations":"The group sizes are reported inconsistently: the text gives 11 constant and 10 progressive players, but Table 1 gives 10 constant and 11 progressive, and the leg counts (20 and 22) match the table. The abstract gives a 8% constant-group fascicle length increase, while Table 1 gives 7.44%. There is no control group, no injury outcome and no significant between-group difference. The PDF prints the year 2018, while the Crossref record lists 2021; the PDF year is used here.",
   "practicalImplications":"Nordic hamstring training improves hamstring fascicle length and thickness in trained rugby players, and a progressive workload may add to the gains in hamstring strength and hamstring-to-quadriceps balance. Because the progressive advantage was not statistically significant, staff should treat progression as a sensible way to plan the program rather than a proven method to prevent injury.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: Plan Nordic hamstring training as a progressed block, not a fixed set of repetitions, because the progressive group showed larger strength and fascicle gains. The paper shows the progression scheme only in a figure, so copy the exact sets and repetitions from the source rather than from this record.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested risk factors in players without current injuries and reports no rehabilitation, reinjury or return-to-play outcomes, so it cannot show when an injured hamstring is ready for competition."
 }
}

   "abstract":"The authors describe a proximal rectus femoris tendon tear in a professional American football placekicker, with imaging, surgical repair and return to kicking.    "tldr":"A professional placekicker with a near-complete proximal rectus femoris tear returned to pain-free kicking about 6 months after surgical repair. This single case shows one successful surgical route, but it does not settle the choice between surgery and nonoperative care.",
   "methods":"A case report of one professional placekicker, with clinical examination, point-of-care ultrasound and MRI at presentation.    "findings":"Ultrasound showed near-complete disruption of the direct head with about 1 cm of retraction, and MRI showed a high-grade near full-thickness partial tear of the direct and indirect attachments.    "limitations":"Only one athlete is described, and the follow-up is a single point at 6 months with no measured strength values.    "practicalImplications":"For a kicker with a near-complete proximal rectus femoris tear, this case shows a surgical route with progressive hip motion, isometric then eccentric loading, and a return to kicking at about 3 months. The authors stress that the choice between surgery and nonoperative care depends on injury timing, career stage and goals, so staff should use this as one example of the process rather than a timeline to follow.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: This case gives one kicker's sequence after surgical repair: non-weight-bearing for 6 weeks, eccentric strengthening from about week 8 and kicking from month 3. It is useful for planning kicking work after a similar injury, but it is one athlete's timeline, not a standard for placekickers.",
   "rtp":"The study can inform return to sport in one professional placekicker: the authors use pain-controlled hip motion and strength close to the other side as the criterion, and this athlete was kicking pain-free at 6 months. It cannot set a return-to-play timeline for other kickers or for nonoperative management, because it describes one surgical case."

}

   "doi":"10.1249/jsr.0000000000001131",
   "abstract":"The survey measured public knowledge of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), the sources people use, their confidence in that knowledge, and their comfort allowing a child to play a high-contact sport. Average accuracy was 48%, and the most common errors concerned the cause and diagnosis of CTE. Confidence was linked with comfort about children playing high-contact sport, but accuracy was not.",
   "tldr":"Members of the public in this survey were often wrong about CTE, especially its cause and how it is diagnosed, yet those who were more confident in their knowledge were more comfortable letting children play high-contact sport. Television, movies and professional athletes were the sources linked with more accurate knowledge, while social media was linked with less accurate knowledge.",
   "methods":"An online survey of 530 participants was analysed, with 529 reported in the abstract and in Table 1. Participants answered six true/false CTE knowledge items (two adapted from Merz et al. and four from the Sports Neuropsychology Society fact sheet), rated their confidence and comfort on 0 to 100 scales, and estimated the share of their CTE information from each source. Total accuracy and item-level accuracy were calculated, and correlations were used to relate sources, confidence, accuracy and comfort.",
   "findings":"Average CTE knowledge accuracy was 48.02%. Only 33.01% correctly rated that CTE cannot be caused by a single injury, 33.97% that it cannot develop without a head injury, and 33.21% that it can be diagnosed only after death, while 70.69% correctly said it cannot be treated. Confidence was positively correlated with comfort allowing a child to play high-contact sport (r = 0.199, p <= 0.001), but accuracy was not (r = 0.004). Television/movies (r = 0.088) and professional athletes (r = 0.127) were linked with higher accuracy, and social media with lower accuracy (r = -0.181).",
   "limitations":"Participants were self-selected online volunteers and the authors could not control for health literacy, English literacy or computer access. The Discussion says 68.90% believed sport alone could cause CTE, while Table 2 implies about 66% gave the wrong answer on that item (33.97% correct). The PDF prints the year 2024, which matches the Crossref record.",
   "practicalImplications":"Clinicians and sport staff should correct common CTE misconceptions when they talk with athletes and families, especially that CTE comes from a single injury or from sport alone, and that it can be diagnosed in life. Because confidence was not linked with accuracy, staff should not assume that a parent's certainty about CTE reflects correct knowledge.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: This study does not measure training or performance.    "rtp":"This study cannot inform return to sport. It surveys members of the public about CTE and reports no injured athletes, concussion management or return-to-play outcomes."
 }
}

Drafts for Q33–Q40 are written to `drafts/`, and `helpers/d05/` is created. All eight pass the taxonomy and inputs check, with no dashes.

- **Q33**: INCLUDE. Identity matches. Year is 2024 in the PDF vs 2025 Crossref, noted.
- **Q34**: INCLUDE. Identity matches. Year is 2025 in the PDF vs 2026 Crossref, noted. Abstract and Table 1 disagree on age SD (1.6 vs 1.4).
- **Q35**: DEGRADED, doiMissing true, DOI left blank. Identity concern: the PDF is "Power-Time Curve Comparison between Weightlifting Derivatives" (JSSM 2017). The batch externalDoi (10.1123/ijspp.2016-0147) belongs to a different paper, "Force-Time-Curve Comparison Between Weight-Lifting Derivatives" (IJSPP 2016), which the PDF's own reference list cites. Operator should find this article's DOI externally.
- **Q36**: INCLUDE. Identity matches.
- **Q37**: INCLUDE. Identity matches. Sample size is inconsistent within the text (4,149 / 4,141 / 4,071), noted.
- **Q38**: INCLUDE. Identity matches. Year is 2018 in the PDF vs 2021 Crossref, noted. Group sizes conflict between text and Table 1, and the abstract's CTG fascicle figure (8%) differs from Table 1 (7.44%).
- **Q39**: INCLUDE. Identity matches.
- **Q40**: INCLUDE, confidence medium. Identity matches. Relevance judgment call: the sample is the general public, not athletes, so this is the record most open to an (c) exclusion. Also noted: the Discussion's 68.90% figure conflicts with Table 2.
